title: Taking turns, fairly

prereqs.why: The arbiter has exactly one bit of state per lap - where the last grant went - and everything else is a function of it.
The grant is combinational and the pointer is registered, and swapping the two changes when a requester is served.
A combinational grant puts the whole search on the path from req to grant, which is the cost of serving in the same cycle.

statement:
Several requesters share one resource. Write the arbiter that decides
whose turn it is, **round-robin**, so that nobody can be starved.

```systemverilog
module rr_arbiter #(parameter int N = 4) (
    input  logic         clk,
    input  logic         rst_n,   // synchronous, active low
    input  logic [N-1:0] req,
    output logic [N-1:0] grant,   // one-hot, or all zero
    output logic         valid
);
```

`N` is at least 2.

### Precisely

- `grant` and `valid` are **combinational**: a requester that raises
  `req` sees its grant in the **same** cycle, not the next one.
- At most one bit of `grant` is ever high. `valid` is high exactly when
  one is.
- With no requests, `grant` is zero and `valid` is low.
- The arbiter remembers the index it granted most recently. The next
  grant goes to the **first requester at or after the position after
  that**, searching cyclically. Requesters that are not asking are
  skipped, not given a wasted turn.
- `rst_n` is synchronous and active low, and resets the arbiter so that
  index 0 has top priority on the first cycle after it.
- The memory only moves on a cycle where a grant is actually made. Idle
  cycles leave it where it was.

### The sample, with all four asking every cycle

```
cycle   1  2  3  4  5  6
grant   0  1  2  3  0  1
```

### Fairness

The property this buys is that a requester holding `req` high waits at
most `N - 1` grants before being served, whatever the others do. A
fixed-priority arbiter — always granting the lowest asking index — gives
no such bound, and index 3 may never be served at all.
hints: One register and one combinational block. The register is the index granted most recently; everything else is computed from it and from `req`.

The search is over the positions `last+1, last+2, ..., last+N`, all taken modulo `N`. Writing it as a loop over `i` from 1 to `N` with `k = (last + i) % N` gets the wrap for free and visits each position exactly once.
Stop at the first requester found. A loop with no early exit will leave the LAST one set instead, so guard the body with a flag — `if (!valid && req[k])` — or break out.

Reset `last` to `N - 1`, so that `last + 1` is 0 and index 0 has top priority on the first cycle. Resetting it to 0 gives index 1 the first turn, which is the off-by-one the grading testbench looks for.
